Orleans Parish and the City of New Orleans

The parish line and the New Orleans city limit are the same line, a match that dates to 1870. The 2020 census counted 383,997 people here, and the 2025 estimate is 362,184. One local government runs zoning, code enforcement and tax billing, so a seller's paperwork mostly stays in one building.

Who handles property tax

Your bill involves three bodies. The Assessor decides value and signs off on exemptions. The Bureau of the Treasury, a city department, sends bills and takes payment. The City Council acts as the Board of Review when someone contests a value.

OfficeRoleContact
Orleans Parish AssessorSets values, approves homestead exemptions, keeps the roll1300 Perdido St, Room 4E01; (504) 754-8811; info@orleansassessors.com
Bureau of the TreasurySends bills, takes payments, runs tax sales, issues refunds1300 Perdido St, Room 1W40; (504) 658-1712; taxresearchunit@nola.gov
City Council as Board of ReviewHears appeals of assessments, separate from the AssessorHearings at Delgado Community College, City Park Campus
Clerk of Civil District Court, Land RecordsRecords deeds and other property documents1340 Poydras St, 4th floor; (504) 407-0005

A bill that keeps coming after you sold should go to the Assessor, which updates ownership and mailing addresses. Treasury also answers common billing questions on its FAQ page.

Due dates, interest and how to pay

The usual due date is January 31, with 1 percent interest added each month to what is unpaid. Bills typically mail in late December, but timing moves with the city's millage vote and the print schedule. Some years the city pushes the deadline later. Most Louisiana parishes use December 31 instead. Selling in early winter? Trust the date printed on your bill.

A bill that never showed up still earns interest, penalty and costs. Search the tax payment portal for yours, or call (504) 658-1712.

  • Online e-checks cost nothing extra.
  • A third-party fee of about 2.49 percent applies to cards.
  • Regular payments can be cash, check or money order.
  • Partial payments work in person or by mail only. They do not halt interest or tax sale costs.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Orleans Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the assessment works

The Assessor estimates fair market value, and only a slice of it is taxed. A home's land and its residential improvements are each assessed at 10 percent of market value, while commercial improvements are assessed at 15 percent. Millage is then applied to what remains after any exemption.

Homestead exemption and the age freeze

If you own and occupy the house, the homestead exemption removes the first $75,000 of market value (that is, $7,500 of assessed value) from the taxable base.

Orleans is unusual here. The exemption reduces municipal property taxes, which it does not do elsewhere in Louisiana.

  • The exemption is tied to you as the occupant. Whoever buys and moves in files a new application.
  • Without a homestead exemption on your bill, payments first satisfy recorded municipal liens, such as code enforcement liens, and only then your taxes (City Code 6-39(d)). An occupied homestead is spared, except when it holds a short-term rental permit or the lien comes from a Chapter 26 violation.

Owners aged 65 or older with qualifying income may apply for the special assessment freeze. It stops on December 31 of the year of a sale or the owner's death, so it never passes to a buyer.

How to appeal your assessment

Raise it with the Assessor while the rolls are open for public inspection. If you still disagree, file a written appeal with the Board of Review. The City Council posts a calendar each year. In the recent cycle, public inspection began in mid-July and the filing deadline fell in the third week of August. Hearings run in September at Delgado Community College, City Park Campus, and written decisions follow in October. Check the Council appeals page for the current dates.

The Board accepts three kinds of evidence:

  • The recent sale price of your property.
  • Recent sale prices of comparable properties nearby.
  • The opinion of a real estate professional.

Appraisals, insurance policies, photographs and contractor repair estimates all help support a claim of damage or over-valuation. Send the form and every supporting paper together, since an incomplete appeal is denied. A Board decision you dislike can go to the Louisiana Tax Commission, by written appeal within 10 business days of the notice. The Board cannot rule on homestead denials or age freeze decisions.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Orleans Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Act 718 phase-in

Act 718 of 2018 lets homeowners spread a big tax increase over four years when an assessment rose by more than 50 percent in a reassessment year. Qualifying parcels carry an "Act 718" marker on the tax bill.

Orleans was reassessed in two phases: 75 percent of the city for the 2020 tax year and the remaining 25 percent for 2021. Owners without a homestead exemption in the year of implementation do not qualify, and neither do commercial owners.

Someone who buys a property already under Act 718 does not get the phase-in, which means the first bill for the new owner may exceed yours. If an appeal lowers the assessment below the 50 percent threshold, the phase-in ends and a revised bill for the full amount comes due.

Unpaid taxes and tax sales

New tax sale and adjudication rules started on January 1, 2026. Under the earlier system, an owner could redeem for roughly three years after the tax sale certificate was recorded. A valid blight judgment shortens that to 18 months, and adjudications can run three to five years. Call the Treasury for how the current process affects your parcel.

To redeem an older sale, you pay:

  • The amount the tax sale purchaser paid at the sale.
  • Interest of 1 percent per month until redeemed.
  • A 5 percent penalty.
  • The current year's taxes and other debts.

Tax sale costs can also appear as a line on a bill, covering the work of preparing a property for the upcoming sale. A tax sale claim or code lien shows up in a title search, and whoever closes the sale has to account for it.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company or attorney uncovers unpaid taxes and liens and settles them from your proceeds at closing. Ahead of that day, confirm your bill status, any municipal liens and whether your homestead exemption is on file.

Under R.S. 47:1993, Louisiana attaches a lien to each assessed property when the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages. That lien generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances, apart from prior-year rolls and tax lien certificates, so unpaid taxes must be settled before clean title passes.

Land Records, at 1340 Poydras Street, takes deeds weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Certified copies run $30 each plus copy charges. Margins matter: 2 inches at the top of the first sheet and 1 inch elsewhere, or the clerk may reject the document or add a $20 surcharge.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the property tax due date in Orleans Parish?

Bills are usually due January 31, and interest runs at 1 percent per month after the due date. The city does not waive it for a bill that was never received.

Who do I call if I sold my house but still get the bill?

Call the Orleans Parish Assessor at (504) 754-8811. That office handles ownership and mailing address changes and can update the account.

What is the Orleans Parish homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, on a home you own and live in. In Orleans it applies to municipal taxes as well, unlike most of Louisiana.

Can I pay Orleans Parish property tax online?

Yes. Online e-check payments have no service fee, and card payments carry a fee of about 2.49 percent. Partial payments cannot be made online, so those must be mailed or paid in person at City Hall.

How long do I have to appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission?

You have 10 business days after the Board of Review's notice is postmarked or delivered. The appeal must be in writing, and forms are linked from the City Council's appeals page.

Lafayette Parish, LA Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Lafayette Parish, LA Property Tax Guide sale

Selling in Lafayette Parish? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Lafayette Parish?

Which bill applies to your address

Lafayette Parish packs six municipalities into 269 square miles of Acadiana, almost none of it water. The city of Lafayette is both seat and largest town. Broussard (partly in St. Martin Parish), Carencro, Scott, Youngsville and Duson (partly in Acadia Parish) have their own governments, while Milton and Ossun are unincorporated communities.

Where the house stands decides what you pay and to whom. A house in Youngsville, Scott or Carencro is taxed differently from one inside the City of Lafayette or on unincorporated land, so find out whether a town levies tax on you before you open the bill.

ContactDetails
Sheriff tax office916 Lafayette St., Lafayette, 337-236-5400
Assessor(337) 291-7080
Payment deadline without penaltyDecember 31
Homestead exemption$7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of market value)
Tax saleFirst Wednesday in June, online

Paying the Sheriff

About 100,000 notices leave the Sheriff's Office each November. Pay by December 31 to avoid a penalty.

The Sheriff also collects for several towns. Carencro and Youngsville joined the arrangement in 2004, and Scott and Duson followed in 2008. Residents of those places get one combined bill covering town and parish tax, and the Sheriff divides the money afterward. One check does the job.

  • Ways to pay: online at the Sheriff's Web Tax Site, or in person with cash, personal check or credit card.
  • Counter hours run 7:30 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Monday to Thursday and 8:00 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. on Friday.
  • Online e-check and card payments cost a transaction fee.

Inside the City of Lafayette the picture changes: the city sends its own tax bill, so you may owe two payments.

What the Assessor does

The Assessor's role is to identify and value property. It does not decide the size of your bill, since rates come from the city-parish government, school board, sheriff and other taxing bodies.

Values are redone at least once every four years under state law, and can change annually if the market moves. Appraisers lead with comparable sales, then test the result with cost and income methods. The website offers a tax estimator, a property search and a parcel map. Check what the county shows for your house before you talk price with a buyer. An assessment is not an offer, but a wide gap deserves a call.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lafayette Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemptions and the assessment freeze

Most owners use the homestead exemption. A home you live in, with up to 160 acres, gets $7,500 of assessed value (equal to $75,000 of market value) taken off state, parish and special taxes. The owner's pool, pool house or storage shed counts too, but a second dwelling or a commercial building on the land does not.

A separate freeze holds the assessed value at its January 1, 2025 level until the home is sold or remodeled, and it stops at the end of December before a sale. You need a homestead exemption and one of the following:

  • Age 65 or older.
  • A permanent, total disability determined by a court, state or federal agency.
  • A service-connected disability rating of 50% or more.

Adjusted gross income may not exceed $100,000. A freeze does not stop millage changes, so the bill can still rise. Farmland is valued by its use if it covers three acres or more, or if it earned at least $2,000 gross in each of the last four years.

How to appeal your assessment

Talk first to a deputy assessor, and arrive with proof. A reduction requires showing the assessment exceeds market value and why. Accept the deputy's answer and the matter ends there.

Still unhappy? The Lafayette Consolidated Council hears appeals in September on dates it sets in August, and it rules after reviewing your material and the Assessor's. The next level is the Louisiana Tax Commission. Its decisions stand unless you take them to district court within thirty days.

Call the Assessor each summer for the current hearing board and filing date.

Unpaid taxes and adjudication

Past December 31, unpaid tax earns interest, and the house may be offered at the online tax sale on the first Wednesday in June. After a tax sale, the Louisiana Constitution gives the owner three years from recordation to redeem, paying the price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest.

If no one bids, the property is adjudicated. Applicants cannot use Lafayette Consolidated Government's disposition process until it has been adjudicated for three years running. Public bidding opens at no less than 75% of the Assessor's fair market value, and a second round about a month later opens at 33%. Outstanding taxes and liens are waived when the right affidavit is recorded, and applicants are urged to hire an attorney with title experience.

Until the act of sale to the applicant is recorded, the owner can still redeem by paying every tax, lien and fee owed to the city and the Sheriff. It costs far less to clear arrears early.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lafayette Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Before you list

A few chores are worth doing ahead of time. Look up your assessment with the Assessor's property search. Find out whether you hold the homestead exemption or the freeze, since neither carries over to the buyer. Confirm which bill covers your address, and pay each one before December 31 if you can, because the interest clock starts on January 1.

If you are behind, call the Sheriff's tax office at 337-236-5400 for the amount due. If the house sits in the City of Lafayette, ask the city for its figure too. Having both numbers in hand lets you compare a cash offer with a listing sale on the same footing.

Bring the most recent notice to any conversation with a buyer or title agent. It shows the parcel, the assessed value and the amounts billed, which answers most of their first questions before they have to ask.

Selling with taxes owed

What you owe is paid out of the sale proceeds. Your closing agent can order a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901, a document that lists unpaid state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes, leaving out the year of the sale.

A cash buyer needs no mortgage approval or appraisal, so sales burdened by tax bills, an inheritance, tenants or repairs can close sooner. The new owner then files a homestead claim and the Assessor records the change.

  1. Request payoff figures from the Sheriff, and from the city if the house lies inside Lafayette.
  2. The closing agent orders the tax certificate.
  3. At signing, the balance is deducted from what you receive.
  4. Confirm the act reaches the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court for recording. Our clerk guide has the fees and steps.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Lafayette Parish?

The Sheriff's Office tax department mails about 100,000 notices each November and collects payments. The City of Lafayette bills its own city tax separately.

What is the Lafayette Parish tax deadline?

The deadline to pay without penalty is December 31 each year. Unpaid amounts accrue interest and can lead to the tax sale in June.

What is the Lafayette Parish homestead exemption?

It exempts $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of market value, for an owner-occupied home on up to 160 acres. You claim it with the Assessor.

Can seniors freeze their Lafayette Parish assessment?

Owners 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, can apply for a freeze if they hold a homestead exemption and have adjusted gross income of $100,000 or less. It fixes the January 1, 2025 value.

Can I sell my Lafayette Parish house with back taxes?

Yes. The taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Selling before adjudication keeps you in control and stops interest from growing.

Caddo Parish, LA Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Caddo Parish, LA Property Tax Guide sale

Selling in Caddo Parish? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Caddo Parish houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Caddo Parish?

Get My Cash Offer →

Caddo Parish at a glance

Caddo Parish is in the northwest corner of Louisiana, with Shreveport as its parish seat and largest city. The 2020 population was 237,848 across 937 square miles. Bossier Parish lies directly east, across the Red River. Besides Shreveport, the parish has the towns of Blanchard, Greenwood, Mooringsport, Oil City and Vivian and the villages of Belcher, Gilliam, Hosston, Ida and Rodessa, which gives owners several local governments to deal with.

Median household income was $42,003 in the 2020 American Community Survey. An owner on a tight income can fall behind on a bill that arrives once a year, and the parish runs an annual tax lien auction for unpaid balances.

Who handles Caddo Parish property tax?

The Caddo Parish Assessor values every parcel and the Caddo Parish Sheriff collects the parish tax. The Sheriff does not decide how much you owe, and the Assessor's Office is separate from the Sheriff.

  • Assessor: Caddo Parish Courthouse, Room 102, (318) 226-6701 for address changes and value questions.
  • Sheriff's Tax Department: Caddo Parish Courthouse, 1st Floor, 501 Texas Street, Room 101, Shreveport, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM; phone (318) 681-0638 for balances.
  • Mail payments to the Property Tax Dept., P.O. Box 20905, Shreveport, LA 71120-0905.
  • Shreveport city tax is collected separately by the city, at (318) 673-5500, and does not appear on the Sheriff's notice.

Outside Shreveport, nine parish fire districts provide fire protection, and their fees are set by voters in each district. Shreveport residents fund fire service through city taxes instead.

How the Caddo assessor sets a value

Caddo uses three approaches: comparing recent sales, estimating replacement cost less depreciation, and looking at the income a property could earn. A sale made under pressure, such as an owner who needed cash fast, can distort a comparison, so the office studies many sales.

Louisiana then applies a fixed percentage to the market value to reach the assessed value.

  • Land: 10%.
  • Residential improvements, including apartments: 10%.
  • Commercial improvements: 15%.
  • Business movable property: 15%.
  • Public service, excluding land: 25%.

Millage then converts the assessed value to tax. Read your own notice for the rate that applies to your parcel.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Caddo Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemptions and freezes

An owner who lives in the home qualifies for the homestead exemption, which removes parish tax on the first $75,000 of market value. It applies to one home, not to city taxes, and not to fire district fees. File as soon as you become the owner; the exemption stays until the owner changes or the home stops being the primary residence.

  • Disabled veteran owners: a 100% service-connected rating, confirmed by a VA form, can qualify for up to $75,000 of additional homestead.
  • Age 65 and older: a special assessment level freezes the assessed value if adjusted gross income was under $100,000. It is lost if the property is transferred or improvements exceed 25% of its value, and a surviving spouse over 55 can qualify.
  • Disabled owners under 65: a freeze is available with 100% Social Security disability or a 50% service-connected rating, but it must be reapplied for each year.

The office requires proof of the previous year's income, such as a tax return or a Social Security statement.

Assessment and appeal timing

Each year the Caddo assessor opens the books in mid August and closes public inspection at the end of that month. Appeals must be received by 5:00 p.m. on a deadline in early September, and the Board of Review hears them a few days later at the Caddo Commission. Call the office for the current dates.

Timing matters because the open-roll period is when an owner can legally file a protest. Many taxpayers wait for the bill that arrives around the first of December, and the office will discuss the assessment then, but a protest can no longer be filed at that point. Mark the late-August dates in your calendar.

When Caddo Parish property tax is due and what happens when it is late

Caddo taxes must be paid by December 31, and notices are generally mailed in the last week of November. After December 31 the tax is delinquent, with interest of 1% per month. Taxes not fully paid by January 31 add a 10% collection fee, and unpaid accounts after that date add the cost of notices and newspaper advertising.

Caddo Parish Sheriff payment rules
Charge or ruleDetail
Due dateDecember 31
Interest after December 311% per month
Collection fee10% if not fully paid by January 31
Personal or business checksAccepted only until the close of business on the last day of February
Mortgage companiesAsked to pay by December 20; postmarks of December 31 are accepted

Payments post to the account number you give, and a payment to the wrong account is final. Partial payments are allowed, but the unpaid balance keeps growing and the parcel is still offered at the annual auction.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Caddo Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens at a tax lien auction

The Sheriff sells a tax lien certificate at an online auction, held in the summer, and the winning bidder is the person who will take the least ownership interest in the property while paying the full unpaid taxes. That matches the new statewide lien approach that took effect January 1, 2026. A property that draws no bid is transferred to the parish, which can sometimes sell it to a third party.

Adjudicated property can be found through the CPTA Professional Search subscription or by visiting the courthouse; phone requests are not answered. Because the rules changed in 2026, a Caddo owner with a delinquent balance should ask the Sheriff what the lien process allows today.

How Caddo property tax works when you sell

The Sheriff does not split the bill between buyer and seller, so the full year's tax stays on the property until someone pays it. A buyer who closes after January 1 may find the account still in the prior owner's name, and the new owner is responsible for checking what is owed.

  • Get the current balance from the Sheriff's Tax Department before choosing a closing date.
  • Check city tax with Shreveport separately, since it is billed apart from the parish.
  • Ask your mortgage servicer for proof of payment if escrow covers the tax, because the Sheriff posts the first payment it receives and will not reverse a duplicate.
  • Have the new owner file for homestead soon after closing.

A house with taxes behind can still be sold if the title company pays the balance from proceeds. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can close that way without waiting on a lender.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Caddo Parish?

The Caddo Parish Sheriff's Tax Department collects parish property tax at 501 Texas Street, Room 101, in Shreveport, or by mail to P.O. Box 20905. The Assessor sets the value but does not take payment.

Is Shreveport city tax on my Caddo Parish tax notice?

No. The Sheriff's notice covers parish taxes only. The City of Shreveport collects its own tax and can be reached at (318) 673-5500.

When do Caddo assessment appeals close?

Appeals must reach the assessor by 5:00 p.m. on a deadline in early September, after the books open in mid August. Call the office at (318) 226-6701 for the current date.

What are the penalties for paying Caddo tax late?

Interest runs at 1% per month after December 31. A 10% collection fee applies if the tax is not fully paid by January 31, and notice and advertising costs can follow.

Can I sell a Caddo Parish house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. The title company can pay the delinquent tax, interest and fees from the sale proceeds. Get the payoff amount from the Sheriff's Tax Department first.

Jefferson Parish at a glance

Jefferson Parish is the suburban ring west and south of New Orleans, cut in two by the Mississippi. The 2020 census counted 440,781 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 431,398. Of the parish's 665 square miles, only 296 are land. Residents talk about it in two halves: East Jefferson (Metairie, Kenner, Harahan) and the West Bank (Gretna, Harvey, Marrero, Westwego). Much of the housing went up in the postwar subdivision boom, so plenty of houses are now old enough that roofs, wiring and drainage can slow a financed sale.

OfficeLocation and phone
Assessor, West Bank200 Derbigny St., Suite 1100, Gretna, 504-362-4100
Assessor, East Bank1221 Elmwood Park Blvd., Suite 901, Harahan, 504-736-6370
Tax collectorJefferson Parish Sheriff, who collects as ex-officio tax collector
Floodplain Management and Hazard Mitigation504-736-6540

Who sends the bill and who sets the value

The job is divided between two offices. The Assessor decides what your property is worth. The Sheriff mails the bill and takes your payment. Both Assessor offices keep hours 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Sheriff's office collects as ex-officio tax collector, and its website lets you pay property taxes online, with a separate module for homestead and mortgage-company payments.

Homes are assessed at 10% of fair market value. Voters approve millage and a local ordinance sets it, and the tax is that millage rate applied to the assessed value. A home inside a city such as Kenner or Gretna pays several levies at once: the parish, the school board, the city and possibly special districts. Whatever name is on your mailing address, the same offices handle your bill.

The Assessor has to send every assessment change to the Louisiana Tax Commission for approval, which makes the Commission the final administrative stop in a value dispute.

Due dates and penalties

Payment is expected as soon as the notice lands, and a bill turns delinquent after December 31. The 2025 bills went delinquent on December 31, 2025, and a short grace window for payments made or postmarked just after that ran to January 2, 2026. Go by the date on your own notice, since the calendar can move it.

Late bills pick up interest at 1% per month, counted from January 1 until you pay. If you mail a check, a postmark proves you were on time, but getting that postmark on the envelope before the deadline is your problem, not the Sheriff's.

  • The Sheriff takes partial payments, though interest and extra costs (certified mail, advertisements, mortgage certificate fees) keep adding up on the balance.
  • Pay in full before the June tax sale.
  • After several years of unpaid taxes, the sale process can move ownership.
  • If a tax sale does happen, the former owner has three years after it is recorded to buy the property back. The payoff is the sale price, costs, a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest (see this Attorney General opinion).
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jefferson Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to challenge your assessment

Go to the Assessor while the rolls are open for inspection. Once that period ends, the appeal form says, no assessment can be changed. Under R.S. 47:1992.1 the rolls stay open for fifteen calendar days. It opens on or after August 1 and shuts by September 15.

The form is strict. Submit all the requested information, because an incomplete form is denied. You need enough documentation to show the assessment may be wrong, and the office makes no promise to agree to a change.

  • Photos must show the whole structure as seen from the street. Interior damage photos must show the entire room. Photocopied photos are refused.
  • You can attach repair estimates, an appraisal or a letter explaining your case.
  • If you are not the owner, a Tax Authorization Form must accompany the request.
  • File one form per property. The apartment form adds a request for two prior calendar years of income and expense statements, plus occupancy rates.

If the Assessor will not budge, take it to the parish Board of Review. You can appeal that ruling to the Louisiana Tax Commission. Call the Assessor each summer for current Board of Review filing dates.

Homestead exemption

Sign up in person at either Assessor office. You will need your act of sale and a photo ID that shows the home's address. If a married couple owns the house together, one spouse can go alone.

Louisiana's constitution takes the first $7,500 of assessed value off the bill for state, parish and special taxes. That equals $75,000 of fair market value. Once you file, you get a yearly receipt in the mail confirming the exemption stays in place. The Assessor's site also carries separate applications for first responders and volunteer firefighters, with a September 1 filing cutoff for the current tax year.

Your exemption stops when you sell. The next owner, if living there, must file a fresh claim after closing, and the first paper the Assessor asks that person for is the deed.

Storm and flood history

Hurricane Katrina, which made landfall on August 29, 2005, is the reference point buyers and insurers use. The East Bank saw widespread flooding and wind damage, while the West Bank had little to no flooding but plenty of wind damage. Jefferson's levees and floodwalls did not fail, so floodwater could be pumped out quickly.

The parish Department of Floodplain Management and Hazard Mitigation (504-736-6540) can tell you whether a lot sits in a regulated flood zone. If a storm has lowered your home's condition, document it. The appeal form asks for repair estimates and photos, and a damaged house can support a lower valuation during the inspection window.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jefferson Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

A tax bill you have not paid will not stop a sale. The balance comes out of your proceeds at the table. Outside New Orleans, anyone party to an act of sale can ask for a certificate that shows which state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are still unpaid. The sale year itself is excluded (R.S. 9:2901).

The transfer then has to be recorded. Under Civil Code article 3338, a transfer of land does not bind outsiders until it sits in the conveyance records. So the closing attorney or title company files the act with the clerk promptly.

Here is the usual order of events:

  1. Ask the Sheriff's office what is owed on the bill, including interest and costs.
  2. The title company orders the tax certificate.
  3. You sign the act of sale before a notary, and back taxes are deducted from what you receive.
  4. The closing agent records the act. The buyer then files a homestead claim of their own.

If you have back taxes, a storm-damaged roof or a tenant, a buyer who takes the house as-is can be the simpler route. The Sheriff also publishes a list of judicial real estate sales. Look at it if a lender or creditor has already moved against the property.

Frequently asked questions

What office collects property tax in Jefferson Parish?

The Jefferson Parish Sheriff collects it as ex-officio tax collector. The Assessor, with offices in Gretna and Harahan, sets the value, and the Louisiana Tax Commission approves assessment changes.

What is the interest on late Jefferson Parish property tax?

Interest runs at 1% per month from January 1 until the bill is paid. Partial payments are accepted, but interest and costs such as certified mail and advertising keep building.

When can I dispute my Jefferson Parish assessment?

Only during the open-rolls period, which lasts fifteen calendar days, beginning no earlier than August 1 and ending no later than September 15. After it closes, no assessment changes can be made.

Can I sell my Jefferson Parish house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, and a tax certificate under R.S. 9:2901 shows what is outstanding. A cash buyer who closes as-is can still complete the purchase.

Where do I file for a homestead exemption in Jefferson Parish?

In person at either Assessor office, at 200 Derbigny St. in Gretna or 1221 Elmwood Park Blvd. in Harahan. Bring your act of sale and a photo ID showing the home address.

Bossier Parish at a glance

Bossier Parish sits in northwest Louisiana on the east side of the Red River, directly across from Shreveport. Its 2020 population was 128,746, and the 2025 estimate is 131,867. Bossier City is the largest municipality, and Benton is the parish seat, where the courthouse and the assessor's office are found. Haughton and Plain Dealing are the other towns.

Barksdale Air Force Base, about four miles east of Bossier City, anchors the local housing market, and the parish is part of the Shreveport-Bossier City metro area. Age and condition still decide how a buyer prices an older house.

Who assesses and who collects property tax

The Bossier Parish Assessor appraises every parcel, and the Bossier Parish Sheriff collects the tax. The assessor's office is at 204 Burt Boulevard, 2nd Floor, in Benton, open Monday to Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, closed on state holidays. The phone is (318) 965-2213.

The assessor posts a SmartCAMA property search and a GIS aerial map, which let an owner look up a parcel's assessment and ownership before calling. The assessor does not take payment. Pay the Sheriff.

  • Online: the "Pay Taxes" tab at bossiersheriff.com, using the tax assessment number and the owner's last name as printed on the notice. A mobile app offers the same service.
  • By mail: Sheriff's Office, P.O. Box 850, Benton, LA 71006.
  • In person: the Bossier Parish Courthouse at 204 Burt Boulevard, the Viking Drive Substation at 2510 Viking Drive in Bossier City, or the Arthur Ray Teague Substation at 3135 Arthur Ray Teague Parkway in Bossier City, all open 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM on business days.

Property tax dates

The tax year runs from a January 1 lien date to a December 31 payment deadline. The open book period and the appeal dates move with the calendar, so ask the assessor for the current year's days.

Yearly property tax calendar in Bossier Parish
WhenWhat happens
January 1Lien date
April 1Business personal property self-reporting deadline
Late AugustOpen book period, about two weeks
Early SeptemberDeadline to appeal an assessment to the Board of Review (Bossier Parish Police Jury)
The following weekBoard of Review hearing
December 31Property taxes due
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Bossier Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Home value and the homestead exemption

Louisiana assesses land and residential improvements at 10% of market value, and the parish tax is then the assessed value times your millage. Commercial improvements are assessed at 15%.

The homestead exemption exempts the first $75,000 of parish value. Call the assessor at 318-965-2213 to file. The assessor's exemptions page also lists relief for disabled veteran owners and other programs, and the SmartCAMA system shows codes for a senior citizen freeze for those over 65 and for a delayed homestead application.

Before a sale, ask the assessor what exemptions are attached to the file, since an exemption tied to the seller as the occupant will not carry over to a buyer.

How to appeal a Bossier Parish assessment

Review the value during the open book period in late August, then file an appeal with the Board of Review by the early September deadline. The board is the Bossier Parish Police Jury, and it hears cases about a week later.

Come with comparable sales, photos of any damage and any repair estimate. The assessor's office can walk you through its records first. If either side disagrees with the board, the case can continue to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and the Bossier office can explain how that step works.

How does the new Louisiana tax lien process affect an owner?

Since January 1, 2026, Bossier's tax collector no longer sells the property itself for unpaid ad valorem tax. The auction now offers a tax lien certificate that represents the delinquent taxes, interest, penalties and costs. The unpaid tax liability is sold and a lien goes to the buyer, but the property is not sold.

  • Interest can run up to 1% per month without compounding, plus a penalty of up to 5%.
  • The certificate is recorded after the auction, and the owner can still pay until 30 days after service of a petition to enforce the lien.
  • The holder may file suit only after the later of three years from recording or 180 days after the required notices under R.S. 47:2156.

Louisiana Revised Statutes sections 47:2153 and 47:2155 set the notice and certificate rules. Contact the tax collector or an attorney about redemption and enforcement. The certificate is recorded, so it has to be cleared at any sale.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Bossier Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax at closing

The tax for the year stays with the property until someone pays it, so check it before you sign anything. Ask the Sheriff's tax office for the account balance, look for any recorded tax lien certificate, and ask the assessor whether a homestead exemption is attached to the file.

Foreclosure is a separate matter. The Sheriff also runs real estate foreclosure sales, which are listed on its own page, with online bidding handled through Bid4Assets. A homeowner who is behind on a mortgage as well as on tax should read the notices on both lists, because the two processes run on different timelines.

A seller with several problems at once, such as an unfinished repair, a tenant in place and a tax balance, can still sell to a cash buyer who takes the house as-is. The title company pays off the tax from the proceeds at the table, so the sale price must be enough to cover the balance, the mortgage and any lien.

Steps before you list a Bossier Parish house

Work through a short checklist before you accept an offer. First, look up the parcel on the assessor's SmartCAMA search to confirm the owner name, the assessment and any exemption codes. Second, call the Sheriff's tax office for the balance on this year's account and ask whether a tax lien certificate has been recorded against it. Third, if you carry a mortgage, check whether escrow paid the tax and get proof.

Put those answers in front of your closing agent early. The payoff comes out of the proceeds at the table, and a recorded certificate has to be cleared before the buyer gets clean title. If you plan to dispute the value, remember that the open book period is short and the appeal deadline follows within days, so the time to call the assessor is before the books open.

After the sale, the buyer should ask the assessor to update the ownership record and apply for a homestead exemption in their own name. Your exemption does not move with the house.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Bossier Parish?

You pay the Bossier Parish Sheriff, who acts as tax collector. Payment can be made online at bossiersheriff.com, by mail to P.O. Box 850, Benton, LA 71006, or in person at the courthouse in Benton or at the two Bossier City substations.

When is the Bossier Parish appeal deadline?

The open book period runs in late August, and the appeal to the Board of Review is due in early September, with the hearing about a week later. Call the assessor at (318) 965-2213 for the exact days.

When are Bossier Parish property taxes due?

Property taxes are due on December 31 each year.

How much does the Bossier homestead exemption cover?

It exempts the first $75,000 of parish value. Call the assessor at 318-965-2213 to file.

Can I sell a Bossier Parish house with a tax balance?

Yes. The title company can pay the delinquent tax from the proceeds at closing. Get the payoff from the Sheriff and ask whether a lien certificate has been recorded.

Who handles property tax

The Terrebonne Parish Assessor values property, and the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects the bill. The Assessor's office is in the Government Tower in Houma and is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. The Tax Collector's office handles payment of tax bills.

Office or ruleDetail

HoursMonday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Tax due date (state rule)December 31
Interest on unpaid tax (state rule)1% per month
Homestead exemption (state rule)$7,500 assessed value, $75,000 market value

How homes are assessed

Your house is taxed on 10% of what it would sell for, and the state orders a fresh reassessment at least once every four years. Each taxing body then applies its own millage rate to that assessed figure. A mill is $1 for each $1,000 of assessed value, which makes a 20-mill levy $20 per $1,000.

Louisiana tax bills combine levies from several taxing bodies, and which ones appear depends on the address. A house inside Houma and one on a bayou road can carry different totals. The Assessor and the Tax Collector can tell you which levies apply to yours.

  • Check the parcel record for the taxing districts listed.
  • Compare last year's bill with this year's assessed value.
  • Ask the Tax Collector about any special districts that apply.

How to appeal your assessment

Use the public inspection period to look over your assessment. If the number seems wrong, take it to the local Board of Review. The inspection period is usually August 15 to September 15.

  • Pull your parcel record and check the facts on it.
  • Collect evidence such as a recent appraisal, damage photos or repair estimates.
  • Contact the Assessor before the Board of Review deadline, which varies by year.

An owner who loses at the Board of Review can go on to the Louisiana Tax Commission and then to court. Damaged houses give owners the strongest cases, which makes a Hurricane Ida repair file worth keeping.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Terrebonne Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When tax is due and what if you miss it

The bill arrives by mail in December and must be paid by the 31st. Every month after that adds 1% interest.

A balance that stays open can end with the property sold at a tax sale. The owner then gets three years to redeem it. Think of that as a last-resort cushion, since costs and interest grow all the while.

If you are selling, closing takes care of the balance out of your proceeds. Ask the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230 for a payoff letter so the title company has an exact figure.

Reading your bill, step by step

A Terrebonne bill looks dense, but five checks cover most questions.

  1. Confirm the owner name and the parcel description match your deed.
  2. Find the assessed value, which should be about a tenth of fair market value.
  3. Look for the homestead exemption. It takes $7,500 off the assessed value if you own and live in the house.
  4. List the taxing districts. A house inside Houma may show levies that a bayou road address does not.
  5. Note the due date, December 31, and the interest that starts afterward.

Keep a copy of every bill you pay, since a receipt settles most disputes about whether a year was covered. If something looks off, call the Assessor at 985-876-6620 for value questions and the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230 for payment questions. They are separate offices, and each can only fix its own part.

A buyer's title company will pull the same record, so errors that you fix now do not become surprises at closing.

Flood zones and storm history

Rain here runs about 65 inches a year, mostly from June through September, and Houma sits about 10 feet above sea level. Low ground and heavy rain make flood questions part of nearly every sale. Check where your parcel falls on the current FEMA flood map before you list, because buyers and insurers will.

On August 29, 2021, Hurricane Ida struck as a Category 4 storm, with 150 mph winds at landfall near Port Fourchon, and it damaged or destroyed many houses in Houma. Francine followed, coming ashore in the parish on September 11, 2024. Buyers of houses from that stretch ask what was fixed and who did the work, so pull together your repair files and insurance claims early.

The parish had 109,580 people in the 2020 census and an estimated 104,163 in 2025, with 33,406 of them in Houma. Bayou Cane is the largest unincorporated area next to the city.

What to gather before selling with tax due

Four documents make a sale move: a tax payoff, the parcel record, your deed and any storm repair papers. With them in hand, a buyer or title company can get to work right away. Here is where each one comes from.

  • Tax payoff or bill: the Tax Collector, 985-857-0230.
  • Assessment and parcel record: the Assessor, 985-876-6620.
  • Recorded deed and mortgage history: the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court.
  • Flood zone status: the current FEMA flood map for the parish.

If you are behind on tax and the house is also in poor repair, say so up front. A buyer who knows the full picture can set a price and a timeline that account for it.

What a cash sale skips

A conventional sale asks the house to pass an appraisal and the buyer's inspection, and lenders often refuse to fund a house with open storm damage. A cash buyer does not need that approval, which is why cash is common for damaged Terrebonne houses.

It does not skip the public records. The title company still searches the Clerk of Court's records, confirms the tax status with the Tax Collector and records the new deed. Your part is to have the payoff, the parcel record, your deed and the repair papers ready.

Compare any cash price with what listing would leave you after repairs, carrying costs and commissions, then decide.

Selling a storm-damaged house with tax owed

Plenty of Terrebonne owners are dealing with a tax balance and a storm-battered house at once. Selling as-is for cash can solve both. The buyer takes on the repairs, and the title company settles the tax out of the proceeds.

  • Get your tax payoff in writing.
  • Collect roof and repair records from Ida or Francine.
  • Check flood zone status on the current FEMA map.
  • Record the sale with the Terrebonne Clerk of Court after closing.

The deed must name who is responsible for property taxes, so the buyer's bill goes to the right address next December.

Expect the title company to ask for the payoff first. Once it has a number, it can schedule the act of sale, pay the balance from your proceeds and send the rest to you. Handing it the parcel record and your deed on day one saves a round of phone calls. Heirs and owners who live out of state can do all of this by phone and email, since the Assessor, the Tax Collector and the Clerk of Court each take requests without a visit.

Who collects property tax in Terrebonne Parish?

The Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects it. You can reach the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230.

When is Terrebonne Parish property tax due?

State rules set the due date at December 31. Interest of 1% per month starts after that.

What is the homestead exemption in Terrebonne Parish?

For an owner-occupied home, it takes $7,500 off the assessed value. That equals $75,000 of fair market value.

How do I appeal my Terrebonne Parish assessment?

Review it during the roll inspection period and then appeal to the Board of Review. The inspection window is usually August 15 to September 15.

Can I sell a hurricane-damaged house in Terrebonne Parish?

Yes. An as-is sale works, and any unpaid tax is paid out of the proceeds when you close.

Selling in Ouachita Parish? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Ouachita Parish?

Ouachita Parish at a glance

Up in the north of the state, Ouachita Parish is anchored by Monroe, its seat and biggest municipality, with West Monroe facing it across the Ouachita River. Those two are the only cities. Richwood and Sterlington are the towns. The 2020 census counted 160,368 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 158,542. Unincorporated communities that show up on property records include Bawcomville, Brownsville, Calhoun, Claiborne, Lakeshore and Swartz.

The housing stock reflects several growth waves, the first tied to the natural gas field found in 1916. Whatever decade your house comes from, buyers will quiz you on roof, wiring and plumbing. School district follows the address, with the Monroe City School System inside Monroe and the Ouachita Parish School Board elsewhere, so confirm yours before you describe schools to anyone.

Who handles property tax

Think of it as a hand-off: the Assessor decides what the property is worth, then the Sheriff collects. State law sets the outline and the Tax Commission writes assessment rules, while the police jury, school board and similar bodies pick the levies printed on your bill.

OfficeRoleHow to reach it
Ouachita Parish AssessorValues all taxable property and tracks homestead exemptionsRecords searchable online
Ouachita Parish Sheriff, Civil/Tax OfficeCollects as ex-officio tax collector(318) 324-2536; pay by mail, in person or online
Board of ReviewFirst appeal step after the AssessorDates come from the Assessor
Louisiana Tax CommissionSecond appeal stepState agency

Useful websites: opassessor.com offers a property search, an interactive map, millage rates by ward and a tax calculator, and opso.net carries the Sheriff's tax information.

How your assessment is figured

Your tax starts with fair market value times a percentage fixed by law. Land and residential improvements both come in at 10 percent. Commercial property and personal property are assessed at 15 percent, except commercial land, which stays at 10 percent.

The maximum homestead exemption, $7,500, is subtracted from assessed value before millage is applied. City taxes are not reduced by it, which is why a house in Monroe or West Monroe can have a bigger total bill than a similar one outside the city limits.

A reassessment is required at least every four years, and a sale or change to the property can trigger one sooner. New buyers are asked to fill out a Sales Questionnaire, which the Assessor uses to check fair market value.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ouachita Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Due dates and late taxes

Under the general state rule, December brings the bill and December 31 is the deadline. Late balances add 1 percent interest per month. The Sheriff's Tax Office accepts mail, walk-in and online payments.

If the notice never reached you, you still owe the tax. Contact the tax collector for the amount.

  • One mailing per year, in December.
  • Interest on late balances: 1 percent a month.
  • Unpaid property may go to a tax sale. For immovable property sold that way, the debtor has three years to redeem.
  • Foreclosure and seizure sales belong to the Sheriff's Civil Division, which auctions on Wednesday mornings at 10 a.m. on an online platform.

How to challenge your assessment

Your first stop is the Assessor. The ladder after that runs from the Ouachita Parish Board of Review to the Louisiana Tax Commission to the courts.

Show proof that the value is off. Boards in Louisiana typically accept recent sale prices, an appraisal or photographs of damage. Outside Orleans Parish the tax roll is open for public inspection from August 15 to September 15. Miss the window and you usually wait a year.

Homestead exemption and the age freeze

Two breaks matter most: the homestead exemption and the assessment freeze for older owners. The exemption takes $7,500 of assessed value ($75,000 of market value) off an owner-occupied home and can reach up to 160 acres containing the residence.

The Assessor's website has an application postcard and a page on the Special Assessment Value Freeze for owners 65 and older. A disability rating of at least 50 percent that is service connected can also qualify, within an income limit. Both benefits belong to the person living in the home, so whoever buys must apply on their own.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ouachita Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a seizure or foreclosure is involved

Sheriff sales are public, and the Civil Division advertises each one in the legal section of a local newspaper before auction. The division handles writs of seizure and sale, garnishments, attachments and writs of possession. If a creditor has already moved against your house, the recorded seizure limits what a buyer can do, so talk to an attorney about timing before you sign a contract.

A seller who is behind on taxes, facing a seizure and carrying repairs often has more choices before the auction date than after it. Contact the Tax Office about the balance, then decide whether to list the house, sell it as-is for cash or work out a payment plan with the creditor.

What buyers will ask about your taxes

Expect three questions. Is the bill current? Does the homestead exemption or freeze stay with the house? What will the first bill look like after the sale? Your own exemption ends when you move out, and the new owner applies separately, so the first bill may be higher than yours. Having the last bill, the parcel number and the Assessor's property search page ready makes those answers quick.

A reassessment can follow a sale, which is another reason the Sales Questionnaire matters. Buyers who know this ahead of time are less likely to renegotiate late in the process. Share the exemption rules with them up front, including that the exemption does not reduce city taxes, and a house inside Monroe or West Monroe will not surprise anyone with its bill.

Selling with taxes owed

A tax debt attaches to the property, and it has to be cleared before clean title can pass. La. R.S. 47:1993 says the delivered assessment roll operates as a lien and privilege on every assessed property, usually ahead of other encumbrances.

Your closing attorney or title company requests a payoff from the Sheriff's Tax Office and settles it out of your proceeds. The deed is then recorded with the clerk of court on South Grand Street in Monroe. A house with a mortgage, back taxes and needed repairs makes for slower title work, so begin the payoff request early.

  1. Look up your parcel on the Assessor's site to check the owner and homestead status.
  2. Phone the Tax Office, (318) 324-2536, for the balance.
  3. Hand the title company that figure and any survey.
  4. At the table, the balance is deducted and the deed is sent for recording.

Any error you spot in the first step is cheaper to fix before the buyer's side finds it.

Frequently asked questions

When are Ouachita Parish property taxes due?

The general Louisiana rule is December 31, and late balances accrue 1 percent interest per month. Call the Sheriff's Tax Office at (318) 324-2536 to confirm the deadline for your bill.

Who collects property tax in Ouachita Parish?

The Ouachita Parish Sheriff, acting as ex-officio tax collector. You can pay by mail, in person or online through the Sheriff's website.

What is the Ouachita Parish homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value, equal to $75,000 of fair market value, on an owner-occupied home. It does not apply to city taxes.

How do I appeal my Ouachita Parish assessment?

Meet with the Assessor, then appeal to the Ouachita Parish Board of Review, then to the Louisiana Tax Commission.

Do I owe property tax at closing in Ouachita Parish?

Unpaid taxes are a lien and must be cleared for clear title, so the balance is normally paid from the sale proceeds. Your closing attorney or title company requests the figure from the Tax Office.
